transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-04-18 15:00 PDT
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Tom (CTO - Sandpiper), Priya (Head of ML), Ellen (CFO), Marcus (Infra)

Summary:
Short intake to understand Sandpiper's cost constraints, latency targets, and which deployment mode (hosted / dedicated / private) makes sense for their upcoming pilot. Discussed per-token economics, batching and prefix/KV caching levers, reserved capacity, and compliance asks (SOC2, KMS). Agreed to send pricing comparisons and a benchmark template; pilot scoping meeting to be scheduled.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and request profile
- Cost sensitivity and budget lanes
- Latency SLOs and 95/99th targets
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
- Batching, caching, and quantization options to hit unit-econ
- Security/compliance: SOC2, SSO, KMS, data residency

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check, is now still good?
[00:06] Tom (CTO): Yep, all good. We got about 50 minutes, is that right?
[00:09] Alex (AE): Yep, 50-55. We'll be focused: get your workload, budget lanes, and we'll recommend hosted vs dedicated vs private for a pilot. Maya and Jordan will handle the technical bits.
[00:21] Maya (SE): Hi all. I'll jump in on the tradeoffs — batching, caching, and what we typically see on unit economics.
[00:26] Priya (Head of ML): Great, quick background: Sandpiper runs a paraphrasing and summarization pipeline for client docs. Peak qps for the front-end is about 80 requests per second, average sequence lengths around 400 tokens, but we do long docs as well — tail goes to 2k tokens for certain flows. Latency targets: interactive UI < 1.2s p95, background jobs can be higher.
[00:50] Ellen (CFO): To add, budget for the pilot is tight — roughly $8k/mo we'd like to stay under initially.
[00:56] Jordan (SE): Okay, that's helpful. When you say 80 qps, is that sustained or bursty?
[01:02] Priya: It's bursty. Sustained baseline is more like 20-25 qps, with spikes to 80 during some flows.
[01:08] Marcus (Infra): We are on AWS, VPC peering is possible, and we have strict egress rules — so private deployment might be a requirement depending on data residency.
[01:17] Maya: Good, that lines up with two common paths. If you want lowest friction and faster time-to-value, hosted Redwood is simplest. But given burstiness and cost sensitivity, Dedicated reserved capacity or Private (VPC) could make sense. We'll run numbers.
[01:29] Tom: The CFO is watching the unit-econ pretty closely. We need something we can predict.
[01:33] Ellen: Exactly. If we go hosted, what's the per-token range? And how much can batching and caching realistically save us?
[01:41] Alex: I'll give a high level: hosted per-token for a 7B-ish open model is roughly $0.0003 to $0.0006 per generation token depending on throughput and reserved commits — this is illustrative. Dedicated reserved instances can push unit cost down materially — maybe 30-60% lower depending on utilization. But the jump is upfront commit versus pay-as-you-go.
[02:00] Priya: Can you break that down by per-inference example? Our average prompt+response is around 600 tokens.
[02:06] Maya: So at 600 tokens, at $0.0004/token, that's about $0.24 per inference. With batching and prefix or KV caching we often get 2-4x effective savings for repeated contexts. For example, for QA over the same doc set, KV caching can avoid re-computing prefixes which drops token work by 40-70% depending on cache hit rates.
[02:29] Tom: But what's the latency impact when batching? Our UI is sensitive to 95th latency.
[02:35] Jordan: Good question. Continuous batching typically adds a small scheduling delay — e.g., 5-25ms for micro-batching at high throughput — but larger micro-batches may add tens to hundreds of ms if you optimize purely for throughput. The trick is dynamic batching with latency SLOs: Redwood runtime prefers latency-first buckets and will batch when it doesn't violate SLO.
[02:52] Priya: So is there a recommended configuration for our mix: 20 sustained qps, bursts to 80, average seq 400, p95 target 1.2s?
[02:59] Maya: For that profile, a dedicated pool with autoscale and burst capacity is often the best cost/latency mix. It gives predictable unit cost for the sustained load and lets us absorb spikes by bursting to reserved or hosted fallback.
[03:13] Tom: Fallback to hosted? Can you explain how that routing works?
[03:16] Alex: Sure — Redwood supports smart routing policies. You can route by policy: latency, cost, or region. For example, primary route to Dedicated (reserved) and fallback to Hosted when capacity saturated. There's also model variant fallback — lower-cost quantized model during overloads. That keeps availability up while controlling cost.
[03:33] Ellen: That sounds promising. But on numbers: how much are we realistically saving with caching? You said 40-70% — is that typical?
[03:40] Maya: It depends on hit rate. For document-based ops where prefix tokens repeat a lot, we see hit rates 60-80% and effective token reduction of 50-70%. For open-ended generation it's lower. We'll need your request mix to estimate.
[03:53] Tom: We'll share request traces.
[03:55] Marcus: Quick aside on on-prem/private: our security team wants KMS control. If we go private, can we bring our own KMS/HSM?
[04:02] Jordan: Yes, Private deployments support customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs. But you'll lose some convenience of hosted upgrades — though Redwood's private control plane minimizes differences.
[04:13] Priya: On quantization — can we safely run 4-bit or 8-bit models to reduce cost? Any fidelity hit for summarization tasks?
[04:21] Maya: For summarization, 4-bit quantization can be fine but depends on model family. We recommend evaluating on your prompt set; Redwood Optimize suggests quant profiles by workload. Often 8-bit is a safer first step with minimal quality regression. We'll provide sample eval templates.
[04:34] Ellen: About pilot economics — if we keep within $8k/mo, what's feasible?
[04:38] Alex: With caching and batching optimization, a hosted pilot for the lower-tier model could stay in that lane if you aggressively cache and prioritize background jobs. But for interactive UI with your p95, you might need dedicated to guarantee cost predictability for sustained baseline. We'll put concrete cost scenarios in the pricing sheet.
[04:56] Tom: For the dedicated route, what's the commit sizing approach? We can't guess perfectly what utilization will be month 1.
[05:02] Jordan: Typical approach: estimate baseline sustained tokens and commit for 60-80% of that. Use autoscaling for spikes and short-term burst credits. Redwood also supports monthly true-ups and flexible ramping in the first quarter of a pilot.
[05:17] Priya: What about model selection? We sometimes prefer a slightly larger model for quality. How does that affect unit cost?
[05:22] Maya: Larger models increase token cost and latency. A 13B model could be 2-3x the per-token cost of a 7B, depending on hardware. But with quantization and batching both can be made more economical; it's a quality vs cost tradeoff.
[05:36] Ellen: Compliance — SOC2 is a hard requirement. We also need SSO, RBAC and audit logs. Any gotchas?
[05:43] Alex: Hosted supports SOC2, SSO via SAML, RBAC, and audit logs — we send the SOC2 pack. For Private you get more control (VPC, KMS). We'll share the security pack now.
[05:54] Tom: Are there latency guarantees in the Dedicated SLA?
[05:58] Jordan: SLA typically covers uptime and target latency bands for reserved capacity; specific p95 numbers vary by commit size and model family, we'll include the SLA excerpt in the docs.
[06:08] Priya: On routing — if we route low-priority workloads to a quantized variant to save cost, what's the failure mode? Any quality regressions or hallucinations?
[06:17] Maya: There's always some quality drop with quantization or smaller models. We recommend fallback evaluation and automatic rollback if eval metrics drop. Redwood Optimize ties quality monitoring to prompt sets and can alert on regressions.
[06:29] Ellen: Ok. Can you give an example cost scenario: hosted vs dedicated for our baseline 25 qps sustained with 400 token avg?
[06:36] Alex: Rough sketch: Hosted (pay-as-you-go) — assume $0.0004/token -> 400 tokens * 25 qps * 3600s * 24h ~ this is huge, but pilot scaled down. For monthly math: tokens/month = 25 qps * 400 tokens * 3600 * 24 * 30 = 25*400*2,592,000 ~ that's way too big, sorry let me reframe with per-month: 25 qps * 400 tokens * 3600 * 24 * 30 = 
[07:02] Speaker 3: [overlap] Alex: math is rough in my head — we'll send a spreadsheet.
[07:06] Priya: Yes please send the spreadsheet.
[07:08] Maya: We'll do an accurate tokens/month calc with your real qps distribution. The high level: Dedicated reserved capacity reduces effective per-token cost by improving GPU utilization via continuous batching and reserved throughput; savings increase as utilization rises. If your utilization is low, hosted may actually be cheaper.
[07:25] Marcus: For pilot we can probably limit sustained usage windows to reduce commit needs. We can also move large background jobs to off-peak.
[07:32] Ellen: That helps. What about burst capacity billing — do we get billed extra for bursts above commit?
[07:37] Jordan: Yes, bursts above reserved are billed at overage rates or served by hosted fallback depending on your routing. The pricing sheet will show overage rates and burst bucket options.
[07:47] Tom: Regarding benchmarks — what do you need from us to run a throughput / latency estimate?
[07:51] Maya: We need: 1) qps distribution over a day (minute granularity ideal), 2) sequence length histogram (prompt and response), 3) target latency percentiles, and 4) any pinned models you prefer. With that we can run an internal capacity/ cost sim and recommend commit sizing.
[08:07] Priya: We'll export traces — will do that by end of week.
[08:10] Alex: Great. A few security notes in-line: if you require data to never leave the VPC, Private or Dedicated with VPC-only routing is required; hosted may be acceptable if you can use Customer-managed encryption keys and strict retention policies.
[08:25] Ellen: How long to stand up Dedicated for a pilot?
[08:28] Jordan: Typical lead time is a couple of weeks after contract for reserved capacity; private on-prem can be longer. Shorter if we use hosted fallback and start the pilot hosted while Dedicated is being provisioned.
[08:39] Tom: Any pitfalls customers hit on caching configuration?
[08:43] Maya: Common pitfall: over-relying on prefix caching without instrumenting cache hit rates; poor eviction policies can cause stale performance. Also ensure your prompts are normalized — small token differences reduce hit rates. We'll provide recommended TTLs and normalization patterns.
[08:58] Priya: On billing — do you expose token-level breakdowns per route/model in the console?
[09:02] Alex: Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route and model, plus tracing hooks. That's helpful for figuring out which endpoints to optimize.
[09:12] Ellen: Nice. Competitor check: how do you compare to Anthropic or OpenAI?
[09:16] Alex: Anthropic/OpenAI are model/cloud providers; Redwood is a serving platform — we onboard models and optimize inference across environments. For some customers, Anthropic models are available as model choices; cost/latency tradeoffs follow the same levers.
[09:28] Marcus: On the private option, we need SSO integration with our Okta tenant. Is SAML supported?
[09:33] Jordan: Yes, SAML SSO with IdP like Okta is supported for both Hosted and Dedicated control planes. For Private deployments, integration is done via your control plane config.
[09:41] Tom: Any case studies for similar sized consultancies or startups?
[09:45] Alex: We have a couple anonymized case studies — one retail data provider cut token costs ~45% after batching and caching and moving to Dedicated. We'll link that.
[09:55] Priya: Can we try a mixed routing: UI routes to dedicated with strict latency SLOs; background jobs route to quantized hosted pool?
[10:02] Maya: Absolutely — that's a common pattern. You'd get guaranteed latency for UI, and background costs minimized. Redwood routing policies can implement that.
[10:10] Ellen: Perfect. So next steps recap?
[10:13] Alex: We'll 1) send a tailored pricing sheet with hosted vs dedicated scenarios and overage rates, 2) share SOC2/security pack and KMS notes, 3) send benchmark template, and 4) schedule the pilot scoping call with infra and ML (proposed week of Apr 27).
[10:29] Tom: Sounds good.
[10:31] Priya: We'll send the request traces by Apr 21.
[10:34] Alex: Great — action items captured. Thanks everyone.
